The dwarf caiman Paleosuchus palpebrosus exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its diminutive size and occupation of well‑shaded, fast‑flowing streams across the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Freshly hatched neonates emerge from parchment‑shelled eggs with a snout‑vent length of 13 cm [Lb = 13 cm], a measurement that places them among the smallest of extant crocodilians. This modest starting length is paired with a wet weight at birth of 50 g [Wwb = 50 g], a value that falls at the lower end of the 46–55 g range reported for this species. The incubation period required to reach this hatching stage is quite prolonged; when eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], development from oviposition to eclosion requires approximately 91.5 days [ab = approximately 91.5 days]. Embryogenesis at this relatively cool thermal regime proceeds slowly, a pattern consistent with the extended incubation intervals documented in other alligatorids that nest under dense canopy cover where solar warming is limited.

This delayed onset of breeding coincides with the achievement of approximately 60 cm [Lp = approximately 60 cm] in snout‑vent length, a size threshold that marks the transition from the pre‑reproductive juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase. Females that have attained this length are physiologically capable of producing their first clutch, though field observations suggest that not all individuals breed immediately upon reaching this size, as resource acquisition and territory quality may further modulate the timing of the first reproductive event. The relatively late age at first reproduction contributes to a generation time that is long for a crocodilian of this small adult body size.

Adult body size in this species is notably dimorphic, with males attaining substantially larger ultimate dimensions than females. The ultimate snout‑vent length recorded for females reaches approximately 77 cm [Li = approximately 77 cm], corresponding to a total length of around 120 cm, whereas males can achieve a final snout‑vent length of 91.5 cm [Li = 91.5 cm], equivalent to a total length approaching 140 cm. This disparity is accompanied by a marked difference in body mass: the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown female is approximately 12,000 g [Wwi = approximately 12,000 g]. This skeletal and mass dimorphism likely arises from differing selective pressures on the two sexes, with male body size being linked to competitive success during the mating period while female size is more closely tied to fecundity and the physical capacity to excavate and defend a suitable nest mound along stream banks.

Under maintained captive conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Paleosuchus palpebrosus has been quantified through detailed observations of clutch production. Females typically lay between 10 and 25 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 10 and 25 eggs per clutch], and they can produce from 1 to 3 clutches annually [F_R_i = 1 to 3 clutches annually] at this temperature. The total annual egg output is thus a function of both clutch size and the number of nesting events per year. These reproductive metrics place the species at the lower end of fecundity among crocodilians, a pattern that aligns with its small body size and the relatively high investment per offspring implied by the substantial yolk content of each egg. The temperature‑dependence of nesting frequency is evident in captivity, where thermal stability allows for consistent multi‑clutch production that may be less predictable in the variable thermal environment of natural stream habitats.

Longevity records indicate that Paleosuchus palpebrosus possesses an extended lifespan for a vertebrate of its modest stature, with a maximum documented lifespan of 53 years [am = 53 years] when maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This exceptional longevity is accompanied by a slow, steady growth trajectory that continues well after the onset of reproduction, a pattern that is typical of crocodilians but particularly pronounced in this species. The combination of a small adult body size, a late age at first reproduction of approximately eight years [tR = approximately eight years], and a maximum lifespan exceeding five decades results in a life‑history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and repeat breeding over a single, high‑fecundity at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] reproductive bout. Such a strategy is likely adaptive in the stable, resource‑limited environments of shaded forest streams where juvenile mortality may be high but adult survivorship can be maintained through low metabolic demands and effective predator avoidance from a young age.
